chapterInsights.title: Introduction to Economics & Scarcity
outcomes: Define economics and scarcity
Calculate opportunity cost
Identify the four factors of production
formulas: Opportunity cost = Value of next-best alternative forgone

definitions.definition: The fundamental economic problem — unlimited human wants face limited resources.
The value of the next-best alternative sacrificed when making a choice.
Land, Labour, Capital, and Entrepreneurship — the resources used to produce goods and services.

revisionPrompts: Distinguish between a positive and normative economic statement.
Draw a production possibility frontier and explain a point inside vs on the curve.
chapterInsights.saContext: SA's unemployment rate (~32%) illustrates the scarcity of labour market opportunities; government must make difficult trade-offs between health, education and infrastructure spending.

chapterInsights.title: Supply & Demand
outcomes: State the law of demand and supply
Draw supply and demand curves
Determine equilibrium price and quantity
Analyse shifts in demand or supply

definitions.definition: As price falls, quantity demanded rises, ceteris paribus — inverse relationship.
As price rises, quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus — direct relationship.
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied — no tendency to change.

revisionPrompts: List three non-price determinants of demand.
What happens to equilibrium when income rises for a normal good?
chapterInsights.saContext: When Eskom raises electricity tariffs (supply-side cost shock), it shifts the supply curve left for SA manufacturers, raising prices and reducing output.

chapterInsights.title: Elasticity
outcomes: Calculate price elasticity of demand (PED)
Interpret elastic vs inelastic demand
Calculate income and cross elasticity

definitions.definition: Measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price. |PED| > 1 = elastic; < 1 = inelastic.
Measures how demand responds to income changes. Positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods.
Measures how demand for one good responds to price changes in another. Positive = substitutes; negative = complements.

revisionPrompts: If price rises 10% and quantity falls 20%, what is PED?

outcomes: Define and calculate total and marginal utility
State the law of diminishing marginal utility
Identify the condition for consumer equilibrium

definitions.definition: The total satisfaction a consumer receives from consuming all units of a good.
The additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit — MU = ΔTU/ΔQ.
As more units of a good are consumed, marginal utility eventually falls.

revisionPrompts: If TU(3) = 30 and TU(4) = 36, what is MU at Q=4?
Explain why the demand curve slopes downward using utility theory.
chapterInsights.saContext: Diminishing marginal utility explains why SA retailers offer bulk discounts — the 3rd pack of chips provides less utility, so consumers need a lower price to buy it.

chapterInsights.title: Production Theory
outcomes: Define and calculate TP, MP and AP
State the law of diminishing returns
Identify the three stages of production

definitions.definition: The additional output produced by employing one more unit of a variable input (e.g. labour).
Total product per unit of variable input: AP = TP/L.
As more variable input is added to a fixed input, marginal product eventually decreases.

revisionPrompts: Draw the TP, MP and AP curves and explain their relationship.
When does the firm enter stage 2 of production?
chapterInsights.saContext: Load-shedding in SA acts like a shock to fixed input (electricity), reducing TP and accelerating the onset of diminishing returns.

outcomes: Distinguish fixed from variable costs
Calculate TC, ATC, AVC, AFC and MC
Describe short-run and long-run cost curves

definitions.definition: Costs that do not change with output in the short run — e.g. rent, insurance.
Costs that change directly with output — e.g. raw materials, labour.
The additional cost of producing one more unit: MC = ΔTC/ΔQ.

revisionPrompts: If FC=R500, VC at Q=10 is R300, calculate ATC.
Why is the MC curve U-shaped?
chapterInsights.saContext: SA retailers' fixed costs (leases in malls) remain high even when sales drop — understanding fixed vs variable cost is critical for break-even analysis.

Determine short-run equilibrium (P = MC = MR)
Apply the shutdown rule

definitions.definition: A market with many sellers, homogeneous products, free entry/exit, and perfect information — price takers.
A firm with no market power that must accept the market price — horizontal demand curve at market P.
A firm shuts down in the short run if P < AVC — better to produce nothing than to not even cover variable costs.

revisionPrompts: Why is demand perfectly elastic for a single firm in perfect competition?
A firm has P = R20, AVC = R18, AFC = R5. Should it shut down?

formulas: Monopoly equilibrium: MR = MC (but P > MC)

definitions.definition: A market with a single seller of a product with no close substitutes — price maker.
Charging different prices to different consumers for the same product (e.g. student discounts) to capture consumer surplus.
A market dominated by a few large firms with interdependent decisions.

revisionPrompts: Why does a monopoly produce less and charge more than a perfectly competitive firm?
Give a SA example of price discrimination.

flashcards.front: Define opportunity cost.
flashcards.back: The value of the next-best alternative sacrificed when a choice is made due to scarcity.

flashcards.front: Name the four factors of production.
flashcards.back: Land (natural resources), Labour (human effort), Capital (machinery/buildings), Entrepreneurship (organising ability).

flashcards.front: What does a point INSIDE the production possibility frontier (PPF) indicate?
flashcards.back: Productive inefficiency — the economy is not using all its resources, or is using them inefficiently.

flashcards.front: Distinguish a positive from a normative economic statement.
flashcards.back: Positive: factual, testable (e.g. 'Unemployment is 32%'). Normative: value judgement, opinion (e.g. 'Government should reduce unemployment').

quizItems.prompt: Scarcity in economics refers to:
options: A shortage caused by natural disasters
The fact that unlimited wants exceed limited resources
A situation where prices are too high
quizItems.answer: The fact that unlimited wants exceed limited resources
quizItems.explanation: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem — human wants are unlimited but resources to satisfy them are finite.

quizItems.prompt: If a student spends R500 on a textbook instead of a concert ticket, the opportunity cost is:
options: Zero, because studying is more important
quizItems.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative — the concert experience the student gave up.

quizItems.prompt: Which factor of production is rewarded with RENT?
quizItems.explanation: The four factor rewards are: Land→Rent, Labour→Wages, Capital→Interest, Entrepreneurship→Profit.

workedExamples.title: Calculating Opportunity Cost
workedExamples.summary: Calculate the opportunity cost of a student's choice.
workedExamples.problem: Bontle can either work part-time (earning R3 000/month) or study full-time. She chooses full-time study. What is her opportunity cost per month?

steps.label: Identify the choice made
steps.explanation: Bontle chose full-time study.

steps.label: Identify the next-best alternative
steps.explanation: The next-best alternative is part-time work earning R3 000/month.

steps.label: State the opportunity cost
steps.explanation: Opportunity cost = R3 000/month (the income she forfeits by choosing to study).

workedExamples.answer: Bontle's opportunity cost of studying full-time is R3 000 per month in foregone earnings.

flashcards.front: State the law of demand.
flashcards.back: As the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded rises, ceteris paribus (all other factors held constant).

flashcards.front: List three non-price determinants of demand.
flashcards.back: Consumer income, price of related goods (substitutes/complements), consumer tastes/preferences, expectations, number of buyers.

flashcards.front: What happens at market equilibrium?
flashcards.back: Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied (Qd = Qs). The market clears — no surplus or shortage.

flashcards.front: If consumer income rises, what happens to the demand curve for a normal good?
flashcards.back: The demand curve shifts RIGHT (increases) — consumers demand more at every price.

quizItems.prompt: A movement ALONG a demand curve is caused by a change in:
options: The price of the good itself
quizItems.answer: The price of the good itself
quizItems.explanation: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the curve. All other factors cause the curve to shift.

quizItems.prompt: At market equilibrium:
quizItems.explanation: Equilibrium is the market-clearing price where Qd = Qs — no surplus or shortage exists.

quizItems.prompt: If the price of tea rises, what happens to the demand for coffee (a substitute)?
quizItems.explanation: Substitutes move in opposite directions: when tea becomes pricier, consumers switch to coffee — coffee demand rises (curve shifts right).

workedExamples.title: Supply and Demand Analysis — Maize Market
workedExamples.summary: Analyse the impact of a drought on the SA maize market.
workedExamples.problem: A drought reduces maize supply in SA. Show the impact on equilibrium price and quantity using supply and demand analysis.

steps.label: Initial equilibrium
steps.explanation: Maize market starts at equilibrium: Qs = Qd at price P₁.

steps.label: Effect of drought
steps.explanation: Drought destroys crops → supply decreases → supply curve shifts LEFT (from S₁ to S₂).

steps.label: New equilibrium
steps.explanation: At the original price, Qs < Qd (shortage). Price rises to P₂ where the new supply curve meets demand.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.explanation: Equilibrium price rises (P₂ > P₁) and equilibrium quantity falls (Q₂ < Q₁) — bad news for food security.

workedExamples.answer: Drought: supply shifts left → equilibrium price rises, equilibrium quantity falls.

flashcards.front: Formula for price elasticity of demand (PED).
flashcards.back: PED = (% change in Qd) / (% change in P) = (ΔQd/Qd) ÷ (ΔP/P). Usually negative (downward sloping demand).

flashcards.front: If |PED| > 1, demand is _____. If |PED| < 1, demand is _____.
flashcards.back: Elastic (responsive to price). Inelastic (not very responsive to price).

flashcards.front: If price rises 5% and quantity demanded falls 15%, what is PED?
flashcards.back: PED = −15%/5% = −3. |PED| = 3 > 1 → elastic demand.

flashcards.front: What does a positive cross elasticity of demand indicate?
flashcards.back: The two goods are substitutes — when the price of one rises, demand for the other also rises (e.g. Coca-Cola and Pepsi).

quizItems.prompt: Price rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 5%. PED = ?
quizItems.explanation: PED = %ΔQd / %ΔP = −5% / 10% = −0.5. |PED| = 0.5 < 1 → inelastic.

quizItems.prompt: If demand is INELASTIC and price rises, total revenue will:
quizItems.explanation: With inelastic demand, the % price rise > % Qd fall, so total revenue (P×Q) increases.

quizItems.prompt: Income elasticity is NEGATIVE for:
quizItems.explanation: Inferior goods (e.g. low-grade mealie meal) are consumed less as income rises — YED < 0.

workedExamples.title: Calculating Price Elasticity of Demand
workedExamples.summary: Calculate and interpret PED for a SA product.
workedExamples.problem: Petrol price rises from R22/L to R24/L. Monthly petrol sales in a town fall from 100 000L to 95 000L. Calculate PED and classify demand.

steps.label: Classify
steps.explanation: |PED| = 0.55 < 1 → inelastic demand. Petrol has no close substitutes — consumers cut purchases only slightly despite price rise.

workedExamples.answer: PED ≈ −0.55. Petrol demand is inelastic in SA. A price rise increases total revenue for petrol stations.

flashcards.front: Define marginal utility.
flashcards.back: MU = ΔTU/ΔQ — the extra satisfaction from consuming one additional unit of a good.

flashcards.front: State the law of diminishing marginal utility.
flashcards.back: As more units of a good are consumed (holding other goods constant), marginal utility eventually declines.

flashcards.front: If TU(4) = 40 and TU(5) = 46, what is MU at Q = 5?
State the consumer equilibrium condition for two goods X and Y.
flashcards.back: MUx/Px = MUy/Py — the consumer maximises utility when the marginal utility per rand spent is equal across all goods.

quizItems.prompt: Total utility (TU) reaches its maximum when:
options: Marginal utility is at its highest
quizItems.explanation: TU peaks when MU = 0 — consuming the next unit adds nothing. After this, consuming more reduces TU (MU becomes negative).

quizItems.prompt: The law of diminishing marginal utility helps explain why:
options: Firms maximise profit at MR = MC
quizItems.explanation: As more units are consumed, MU falls — consumers are only willing to pay less for additional units, creating a downward-sloping demand curve.

quizItems.prompt: A consumer spends R10 on product X (MU=20) and R5 on product Y (MU=5). Is the consumer in equilibrium?
options: No, because MUx/Px (2) > MUy/Py (1) — shift spending to X
No, because MUy/Py > MUx/Px — shift spending to Y
Yes, as long as total budget is spent
quizItems.answer: No, because MUx/Px (2) > MUy/Py (1) — shift spending to X
quizItems.explanation: MUx/Px = 20/10 = 2; MUy/Py = 5/5 = 1. Consumer gets more utility per rand from X — should buy more X, less Y.

workedExamples.title: Marginal Utility Table Analysis
workedExamples.summary: Calculate MU from a TU schedule and identify equilibrium consumption.
workedExamples.problem: The following TU schedule is given for cold drinks on a hot day: Q=1: TU=20; Q=2: TU=36; Q=3: TU=48; Q=4: TU=56; Q=5: TU=60; Q=6: TU=60; Q=7: TU=55. Calculate MU for each unit and identify when TU is maximised.

steps.label: Identify TU maximum
steps.explanation: TU is maximised at Q=6 (TU=60) where MU=0.

steps.label: Identify diminishing MU onset
steps.explanation: MU falls from Q=1 (MU=20) throughout — diminishing marginal utility applies from the first unit.

steps.label: Interpret Q=7
steps.explanation: At Q=7, MU=−5 (negative) — the consumer is over-consuming and total utility falls.

workedExamples.answer: MU falls throughout. TU is maximised at Q=6 (MU=0). Stop consuming at Q=6.

flashcards.front: Define marginal product of labour (MP).
flashcards.back: MP = ΔTP/ΔL — the additional output produced by adding one more unit of labour.

flashcards.front: State the law of diminishing returns.
flashcards.back: As more units of a variable input (labour) are added to a fixed input (capital/land), marginal product eventually falls.

flashcards.front: When is average product (AP) at its maximum?
flashcards.back: AP is at its maximum when AP = MP (the marginal product curve intersects the average product curve at its peak).

flashcards.front: If labour input rises from 3 to 4 workers and TP rises from 30 to 38 units, what is MP?
flashcards.back: MP = ΔTP/ΔL = (38−30)/(4−3) = 8 units per worker.

quizItems.prompt: The law of diminishing returns states that as more labour is added to fixed capital:
options: Total product eventually falls to zero
quizItems.explanation: Diminishing returns sets in when the variable input (labour) begins to crowd the fixed input — each extra worker adds less output.

quizItems.prompt: If TP = 60 and L = 10, what is Average Product (AP)?
quizItems.explanation: AP = TP/L = 60/10 = 6 units per worker.

quizItems.prompt: In the short run, which input is FIXED?
quizItems.explanation: In the short run, at least one input (typically capital like machinery or buildings) cannot be varied — only labour and materials are variable.

workedExamples.title: TP, AP and MP Table
workedExamples.summary: Calculate product curves from a labour schedule.
workedExamples.problem: A bakery has: L=1: TP=10; L=2: TP=22; L=3: TP=33; L=4: TP=40; L=5: TP=44; L=6: TP=44. Calculate MP and AP for each level of labour.

steps.label: Identify key points
steps.explanation: MP peaks at L=2 (MP=12). AP peaks at L=2-3 (AP=11). MP crosses AP at L=2-3 peak. Diminishing returns begin at L=2.

steps.label: Identify Stage 2
steps.explanation: Stage 2 (rational production): L=2 to L=6 (MP > 0, AP > MP).

workedExamples.answer: MP peaks at L=2, then falls. AP peaks at L=2-3. Diminishing returns begin from L=2 onward.

flashcards.front: How is marginal cost (MC) calculated?
flashcards.back: MC = ΔTC/ΔQ — the change in total cost when output increases by one unit.

flashcards.front: FC = R600, VC at Q=10 is R400. Calculate ATC, AVC, AFC.
Why does AFC always fall as output increases?
flashcards.back: Fixed costs are constant; dividing the same fixed cost by increasing output means AFC falls continuously (hyperbola shape).

flashcards.front: Why is the MC curve U-shaped?
flashcards.back: MC falls initially (increasing returns/specialisation), then rises as diminishing returns set in — mirroring the inverted-U shape of MP.

quizItems.prompt: FC = R1 000, VC at Q = 20 is R600. ATC at Q = 20 is:
Which cost does NOT change with output in the short run?
quizItems.explanation: Fixed costs (rent, insurance, equipment lease) are incurred regardless of output level in the short run.

quizItems.prompt: The ATC curve is U-shaped because:
options: MC pulls ATC down then up as output rises
VC is always greater than FC
quizItems.answer: MC pulls ATC down then up as output rises
quizItems.explanation: When MC < ATC, ATC falls; when MC > ATC, ATC rises. Since MC is U-shaped, ATC follows — pulled by the MC curve.

workedExamples.title: Complete Cost Table
workedExamples.summary: Fill in a cost table and calculate all cost measures.
workedExamples.problem: A firm has FC = R500. VC at Q=5 is R250 and at Q=6 is R320. Calculate TC, ATC, AVC, AFC, and MC at Q=5 and Q=6.

steps.label: Interpretation
steps.explanation: ATC is falling from Q=5 to Q=6 (150→136.7) even though MC (R70) is rising above AVC — the falling AFC is still pulling ATC down.

flashcards.front: List four characteristics of perfect competition.
flashcards.back: Many buyers and sellers; homogeneous (identical) products; free entry and exit; perfect information; firms are price takers.

flashcards.front: What is the profit-maximising rule?
flashcards.back: A firm maximises profit where MR = MC. In perfect competition, MR = P, so profit is maximised where P = MC.

flashcards.front: State the shutdown rule for a perfectly competitive firm.
flashcards.back: Shut down if P < AVC. The firm minimises losses by producing nothing — fixed costs are sunk but variable costs are avoided.

flashcards.front: Why does a perfectly competitive firm earn zero economic profit in the long run?
flashcards.back: Free entry and exit eliminates supernormal profits and losses. New firms enter when π > 0 (price falls); firms leave when π < 0 (price rises). Long-run: P = ATC → π = 0.

quizItems.prompt: In perfect competition, the individual firm's demand curve is:
quizItems.explanation: A price-taking firm can sell any quantity at the market price but nothing above it — demand is horizontal (perfectly elastic).

quizItems.prompt: A firm should shut down in the short run when:
quizItems.explanation: Shutdown rule: if price doesn't cover variable costs (P < AVC), the firm minimises loss by producing zero.

quizItems.prompt: The perfectly competitive firm maximises profit by producing where:
quizItems.explanation: Profit is maximised at MR = MC. In perfect competition, MR = P, so the rule becomes P = MC.

workedExamples.title: Should the Firm Shut Down?
workedExamples.summary: Apply the shutdown rule to a firm's cost data.
workedExamples.problem: A perfectly competitive firm has: P = R25, AVC = R28, ATC = R35. Should it produce or shut down?

steps.label: Apply shutdown rule
steps.explanation: Compare P to AVC: P (R25) vs AVC (R28). Since P < AVC, the firm cannot even cover variable costs.

steps.label: Decision
steps.explanation: Shut down. Every unit produced loses R3 in variable costs plus contributes nothing to fixed costs.

steps.label: What if P = R30?
steps.explanation: P (R30) > AVC (R28) → continue producing. The R2 per unit above AVC contributes to fixed costs. Loss is smaller than if the firm shuts down.

workedExamples.answer: At P=R25 < AVC=R28: shut down. At P=R30 > AVC=R28: continue producing despite ATC loss.

flashcards.front: List four characteristics of a monopoly.
flashcards.back: Single seller; unique product (no close substitutes); high barriers to entry; price maker (faces downward-sloping demand).

flashcards.front: In monopoly, why is MR < P?
flashcards.back: To sell more, the monopolist must lower price on ALL units — so the extra revenue from one more unit (MR) is less than the new price.

flashcards.front: What is first-degree price discrimination?
flashcards.back: Charging each consumer their maximum willingness to pay — the firm captures all consumer surplus. E.g. personalised medical pricing.

flashcards.front: What is deadweight loss in a monopoly?
flashcards.back: The loss of total surplus (value to society) because the monopolist produces less (Qm < Qpc) and charges more (Pm > Ppc) than under perfect competition.

quizItems.prompt: A monopolist faces a ________ demand curve.
quizItems.explanation: The monopolist is the sole supplier — it faces the entire market demand curve which is downward sloping. To sell more, it must lower price.

quizItems.prompt: Compared to perfect competition, a monopoly produces:
options: More output at a lower price
The same output at the same price
Less output at a higher price
More output at a higher price
quizItems.answer: Less output at a higher price
quizItems.explanation: The monopolist maximises profit at MR=MC, which results in lower quantity and higher price than the competitive outcome, creating deadweight loss.

quizItems.prompt: Eskom charging residential customers lower rates than industrial customers for the same electricity is an example of:
quizItems.explanation: Price discrimination involves charging different prices to different market segments — Eskom charges different rates to different consumer groups.

workedExamples.title: Monopoly Equilibrium
workedExamples.summary: Find the monopolist's profit-maximising output and price.
workedExamples.problem: A monopolist has: P = 100 − 2Q (demand/AR) and TC = 200 + 10Q. Find profit-maximising Q, P and economic profit.

steps.label: Find MC
steps.explanation: TC = 200 + 10Q. MC = dTC/dQ = 10.

workedExamples.answer: Q* = 22.5 units, P* = R55, Economic profit = R812.50.

flashcards.front: Define a negative externality.
flashcards.back: A cost imposed on third parties not involved in a market transaction — e.g. a factory's pollution harming nearby residents.

flashcards.front: What are the two characteristics of a public good?
flashcards.back: Non-excludable (cannot prevent non-payers from using it) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's).

flashcards.front: How does a carbon tax correct a negative externality?
flashcards.back: A carbon tax raises the private cost of polluting to equal the social cost (MSC = MPC + MEC), reducing production to the socially optimal level.

flashcards.front: What is the free-rider problem?
flashcards.back: When non-payers cannot be excluded from using a public good, individuals have no incentive to pay — the market under-provides the good.

quizItems.prompt: Air pollution from a factory is an example of:
quizItems.explanation: Factory pollution imposes costs (health, environment) on third parties who are not part of the production transaction.

quizItems.prompt: National defence is a classic example of a public good because it is:
quizItems.explanation: National defence protects all citizens simultaneously (non-rival) and cannot exclude residents from protection (non-excludable).

quizItems.prompt: A negative externality causes the free market to:
options: Produce at the socially optimal level
quizItems.explanation: Producers ignore external costs, so private cost (MPC) < social cost (MSC). This leads to overproduction relative to the socially optimal quantity.

workedExamples.title: Correcting a Negative Externality with a Tax
workedExamples.summary: Analyse market failure and the optimal Pigouvian tax.
workedExamples.problem: A factory produces 1 000 units per day. Private marginal cost = R20, but each unit generates R8 in pollution (external cost). What is the socially optimal output? What tax would correct the externality?

steps.label: Calculate MSC
steps.explanation: MSC = MPC + MEC = R20 + R8 = R28 per unit.

steps.label: Identify the problem
steps.explanation: Firm maximises profit at P = MPC (R20), ignoring external costs. It produces more than the socially optimal level.

steps.label: Find optimal output
steps.explanation: Socially optimal: produce where P = MSC (R28), not P = MPC (R20). Output falls when the 'true' cost is reflected.

steps.label: Recommend tax
steps.explanation: A Pigouvian tax of R8 per unit raises the firm's private cost to R28 = MSC, internalising the externality and reducing production to the social optimum.

workedExamples.answer: Optimal Pigouvian tax = R8/unit (the external marginal cost). This forces the market to produce at the socially efficient quantity.

Chapter-by-chapter teaching focus (derived from the module's own learning outcomes and key definitions):

• Chapter 1 — Introduction to Economics & Scarcity. Emphasise: Define economics and scarcity; Calculate opportunity cost; Identify the four factors of production. Local context: SA's unemployment rate (~32%) illustrates the scarcity of labour market opportunities; government must make difficult trade-offs between health, education and infrastructure spending.

• Chapter 2 — Supply & Demand. Emphasise: State the law of demand and supply; Draw supply and demand curves; Determine equilibrium price and quantity. Local context: When Eskom raises electricity tariffs (supply-side cost shock), it shifts the supply curve left for SA manufacturers, raising prices and reducing output.

• Chapter 3 — Elasticity. Emphasise: Calculate price elasticity of demand (PED); Interpret elastic vs inelastic demand; Calculate income and cross elasticity. Local context: The National Energy Regulator (NERSA) uses elasticity analysis when approving Eskom tariff increases — inelastic demand means large revenue increases are possible.

• Chapter 4 — Consumer Theory & Utility. Emphasise: Define and calculate total and marginal utility; State the law of diminishing marginal utility; Identify the condition for consumer equilibrium. Local context: Diminishing marginal utility explains why SA retailers offer bulk discounts — the 3rd pack of chips provides less utility, so consumers need a lower price to buy it.

• Chapter 5 — Production Theory. Emphasise: Define and calculate TP, MP and AP; State the law of diminishing returns; Identify the three stages of production. Local context: Load-shedding in SA acts like a shock to fixed input (electricity), reducing TP and accelerating the onset of diminishing returns.

• Chapter 6 — Cost Theory. Emphasise: Distinguish fixed from variable costs; Calculate TC, ATC, AVC, AFC and MC; Describe short-run and long-run cost curves. Local context: SA retailers' fixed costs (leases in malls) remain high even when sales drop — understanding fixed vs variable cost is critical for break-even analysis.

• Chapter 7 — Perfect Competition. Emphasise: List the characteristics of a perfectly competitive market; Determine short-run equilibrium (P = MC = MR); Apply the shutdown rule. Local context: Agricultural markets in SA (maize, wheat on SAFEX) approximate perfect competition — thousands of farmers, standardised product, price set by the exchange.

• Chapter 8 — Monopoly & Imperfect Competition. Emphasise: Describe monopoly characteristics and sources of monopoly power; Determine monopoly equilibrium (MR=MC); Explain price discrimination and its types. Local context: Eskom is a natural monopoly in SA — single supplier of electricity. The Competition Commission monitors SA firms like Telkom and Pick n Pay for anti-competitive behaviour.

• Chapter 9 — Market Failure & Government Intervention. Emphasise: Identify sources of market failure; Distinguish between positive and negative externalities; Explain the characteristics of public goods. Local context: SA's national roads are mixed goods. Load-shedding imposes huge negative externalities on SA businesses — estimated to cost the economy R500m+ per day.
